newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks buffeted in another volatile session.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks buffeted in another volatile session.

text.p: The Japanese stock market was buffeted in another volatile session Tuesday, falling sharply and then rebounding in what traders say may represent the end of the frenzied selling -- at least for now.
Brokers said a late wave of buying of blue-chip stocks rescued the market from its initial loss of more than 500 points.
The benchmark Nikkei stock average of 225 leading shares closed 25.66 points lower at 18,093.13.

"Domestic investors, including pension funds and some foreign investors, started buying bellwether issues near the end of the session, helping erase the losses accumulated in the morning," said Akishige Ishikura, an analyst at Dai-ichi Securities.

Stocks rocketed 800 points higher Monday in reaction to last week's sharp selloff and media reports that a senior official of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party called for steps to rescue weak stock prices.

Friday's fall was the largest single-day drop since the Nikkei plunged 1,054.72 points -- or 5.6 percent -- on Jan. 23, 1995, when investors dumped Japanese shares on fears that the Jan. 17 Kobe earthquake would take a heavy toll on the economy.

But the bubble of enthusiasm was popped early on Tuesday by remarks from Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that economic fundamentals were not bad and by the fact that he made no mention of special measures to prop up stocks.
Despite the rebound, many brokers said that perils of another market rout remain, and that only the government could set the market back on its feet.
"What the government needs to do is to take swift action to realise structural reforms in the economy," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute.
Takagi said the government must take some action such as abolishing the securities transaction tax as early as April, and seek early implementation of Japan's planned "Big Bang" financial reforms.

Some traders said the market may already have hit a bottom, but said it is still vulnerable to renewed selling pressure due to lingering worries over the health of the economy and the debt-burdened banking sector.

Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities, said that judging from Monday's rebound and the healthy trading volume on the first two days of the week, the Nikkei may be stabilising, at least for now.
"There is likely to be more weakness in February before book-closing and especially if high-flying U.S. stocks start to falter," he said.
Technical analysts say that the market appears to have found a support line just above the 17,000 point level.

They said stocks could retest recent lows in February, as the market still lacks confidence in Japan's economic recovery, adding that a break through the floor could trigger an accelerated drop to new depths.
